inspection.method: Direct inspection of the official DuckDB repository README, Why DuckDB, concurrency documentation, direct Parquet-query documentation and the current DuckDB v2.0 preview.
gaps: This case focuses on the in-process composition model, not DuckDB's vectorized execution internals or storage engine implementation.
Quack is a fast-moving remote-access surface; exact production v2.0 protocol/deployment semantics should be rechecked when v2.0 stabilizes.

content_map.problem: Analytical work inside scripts, notebooks and applications often pays integration cost to move data into a separate database service before SQL can be useful.
content_map.thesis: DuckDB puts an analytical SQL database inside the host process so applications can query local, host-memory or file data through native clients without requiring a separate database server for the core embedded workflow; the same architecture centers stable read-write ownership in one process, while Quack is adding an explicit remote mode.
sections: MVCC plus optimistic concurrency within the writer process
DuckDB v2.0 preview: Quack/CONNECT remote mode
mechanisms: DuckDB runs inside the same process as the calling application rather than requiring a separate server process for its normal embedded use.
Native clients let Python, R, Java, Wasm and other environments invoke the engine directly.
CSV and Parquet files can be queried directly from SQL; Parquet scans can push projections and filters into the file read.
The core read/write model is process-centered and uses MVCC plus optimistic concurrency control among writer threads in that process.
Quack/CONNECT introduces a remote client-server option without erasing the local in-process mode.
examples: A Python data pipeline can query a DataFrame or Parquet file with SQL without provisioning a remote analytical database.
A desktop or embedded application can ship analytical SQL capability as a library inside the application process.
Multiple writer threads can operate inside the read-write process using MVCC/OCC, while unrelated writer processes require another coordination or remote architecture.
A future/shared deployment can add Quack remote access instead of pretending every DuckDB workload must remain local forever.
claims: DuckDB's core architecture is an analytical in-process database system.
In-process deployment makes host/database data transfer cheap and some host integrations can avoid explicit import/copy.
DuckDB can query CSV and Parquet files directly from SQL and push filters/projections into Parquet scans.
DuckDB's stable writable concurrency model is centered on one process and uses MVCC plus optimistic concurrency control within it.
DuckDB is adding Quack/CONNECT as a client-server mode for v2.0, so in-process is foundational rather than exclusive.
evidence: Official GitHub README and Why DuckDB page inspected on 2026-08-27.
Official DuckDB concurrency and Parquet-query documentation inspected on 2026-08-27.
Official DuckDB v2.0 preview dated 2026-08-17 inspected for the current remote-mode boundary.
assumptions: The workload is analytical rather than dominated by many tiny concurrent OLTP transactions.
Embedding the database in the application process reduces operational or data-movement friction for the target workflow.
The application can accept the lifecycle and concurrency implications of a process-local engine or explicitly choose a remote mode when sharing requires it.
limitations: In-process deployment reduces service boundaries but also couples database lifecycle and resource use more closely to the host process.
The core embedded read-write model is not automatically the right fit for many independent writer processes or OLTP-heavy workloads.
Direct file querying does not remove data-governance, consistency or data-quality requirements and is not always faster than loading data into DuckDB.
MVCC inside DuckDB reinforces a known concurrency primitive but does not make DuckDB's process ownership equivalent to PostgreSQL's deployment model.
Quack/client-server support is actively evolving toward v2.0 and should be re-analyzed after stabilization.
open_questions: Which local data-processing utilities become materially simpler when SQL execution is embedded instead of provisioned as a service?
When does loading Parquet into DuckDB outperform querying it directly for repeated workloads?
How should Quack change the boundary between embedded local analytics and shared database-service architecture once stable?

selection.requested_focus: Understand the architectural value of an in-process analytical database, how this changes data-tool composition, and where the model differs from client/server databases.
coherent_core: In-process is the architectural boundary: the analytical engine lives in the application process.
Native clients and direct file/host-object querying make SQL a composable library capability rather than necessarily a remote service.
That composition reduces setup and data-movement friction for analytical tools.
The trade-off is process-centered write ownership, even though MVCC/OCC supports concurrent writer threads inside that process.
Quack extends DuckDB toward remote access as an additional mode rather than invalidating the embedded model.
prerequisites: difference between in-process and client/server software
drop_notes: Vectorized execution internals are outside this source-focused architectural model.
Benchmark claims are excluded because the product value here is composition, not a speed ranking.
Retrieved workflow/process concepts are rejected as unrelated; only the already-known MVCC concept is reused because DuckDB explicitly documents it in the single-process concurrency model.
connections: PostgreSQL MVCC is reinforced as a general concurrency primitive, but DuckDB applies it inside a different process-ownership and analytical deployment model.
SQLite is an adjacent embedded-database comparison, but DuckDB's primary design center is analytical SQL/OLAP rather than general-purpose application transactions.
